name: Intake and exhaust camshaft gears
what: Two toothed sprockets attach to the ends of the intake and exhaust camshafts.
why: The camshaft gears transfer timing-belt motion to both camshafts and keep their rotation synchronized with the crankshaft.
where: One gear mounts to the exposed end of each overhead camshaft at the timing-belt end of the cylinder head.
installationReason: Fit one sprocket to each camshaft nose. Their teeth engage the timing belt; the alignment marks must be set using the correct B16 service procedure.

guide.overview: The two camshaft gears drive the intake and exhaust camshafts from the timing belt.
guide.operation: The crankshaft drives the timing belt, which turns both camshaft sprockets. Correct alignment keeps valve events synchronized with piston position.
guide.construction: This educational procedural model shows two toothed steel sprockets with central mounting hubs and timing-mark details. It is not a factory CAD reproduction.
guide.specifications: Exact sprocket tooth count, diameter, bolt torque, timing-mark positions, and timing procedure depend on the specific B16 variant and must be verified against its service information.
guide.inspection: Check teeth for wear or damage, inspect the mounting faces and locating features, and verify timing marks and belt alignment using the matching service manual.
guide.failureModes: Damaged teeth, loose fasteners, incorrect timing, or a slipping belt can cause loss of valve timing and potentially severe engine damage.
